reading.body:
Education AI is tracked here through policy, market intelligence, and course listings, not through specific tools or infrastructure.

The four entries point to federal guidance for schools, a market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding and AI learning platforms, and two references to a catalog of courses and credentials. The summary identifies tutoring systems, drafting assistance, and academic integrity policy as the live questions from K-12 through university. That pattern suggests the field is being defined by rules and training pathways more than by named deployments.

For AI scaling, this data offers no direct signal about compute, buildings, or power. It does not list data centers, energy demand, or hardware. What it does show is that education's AI footprint is currently administrative and pedagogical, with procurement and credentialing as the visible pressure points. Readers should not infer infrastructure constraints from this set.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau, 30.0% of firms in Educational services (NAICS 61) answered yes to using AI in the last two weeks, the latest reading, against a prior period figure of 35.5%. The question was first asked in September 2023, and the Census Bureau notes that some values are suppressed. Because the measure covers a two week window, it captures whether AI was in use at all, not how deeply it is embedded or what it cost.

The Department of Education has assembled an inventory of AI use-cases that shows what adoption looks like inside an education agency. Its entries include CAISY, described as enhancing decision-making and operational efficiency through real-time insights, predictive analytics and intelligent automation, Grammarly's AI assistant for written communication, Otter.AI for real-time transcription and collaboration in meetings, interviews and lectures, and AWS Bedrock for building applications on foundation models. Other listed uses are narrower: generating summaries and outlines for projects and presentations, producing code snippets in several programming languages, extracting key points and action items from public documents, generating mock data sets for testing, training employees on prompt engineering, converting data types such as county names into FIPS codes, and drafting outreach strategies, project plans and position descriptions.

The Department of Education's AI guidance frames permissible use, risk and procurement for US education, and its OCIO supports adherence to federal regulations on AI advancement and secure usage in accordance with the Executive Order Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence. The inventory also describes testing filters and data loss prevention by feeding the system fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information. That is the regulatory posture the sources show, an agency documenting its own use-cases while tying them to federal rules.

The World of AI catalogues 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, 3 with public companion code, each with a verified source and re-verified daily. Four are university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285 and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry, DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai and independent researcher Andrej Karpathy. The catalogue describes university courses as generally structured around exam-driven theory and the industry courses as code-first or hands-on, and notes that the data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken.

HolonIQ describes itself as a platform for impact market intelligence covering the global impact economy, and its stated work includes sizing addressable markets, quantifying demand, forecasting scenarios at varying rates of growth, and quantifying impact with rubrics, ratings and scoring to power policy, procurement and investment decisions. It says it serves governments, institutions, technology companies, global firms and investors, and that global media rely on it for insight and data. The excerpt does not give education-specific AI adoption or spending figures.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few narrow conclusions. The Census Bureau figure is a two week usage measure, so it says whether AI is in use, not how much value it returns, and the sources here report no ROI evidence for education. The Department of Education's inventory shows documented uses clustering around drafting, summarization, transcription, code assistance and internal analysis rather than instruction. The guidance ties deployment to federal regulation and procurement review, and the course catalogue shows that most tracked training is free to access but that completion and enrollment data are not reported.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
